$I = \dfrac{Q}{t}$ — charge per second, in amperes.

For a conductor it can also be written $I = nAvq$, in terms of the number density of carriers, the area, the drift velocity and the charge on each.

questions.q: The potential difference between two points is:
questions.solution:
$V = \dfrac{W}{Q}$ — the **energy transferred per coulomb**, in volts.

An **emf** is the same ratio for a source: the energy **given** to each coulomb, rather than taken from it.
options: the energy transferred per unit charge

questions.q: The resistance of a uniform wire is:
questions.solution:
$R = \mathbf{\dfrac{\rho L}{A}}$.

Note that doubling the **diameter** quadruples the area, so it quarters the resistance — the area, not the diameter, is what appears in the formula.

questions.q: The terminal potential difference of a cell is less than its emf because of:
questions.solution:
$V = \varepsilon - Ir$ — some of the emf is spent driving the current through the cell itself.

The 'lost volts' $Ir$ grow with current, which is why a torch battery reads lower under load, and why an old battery with a high $r$ sags badly.

questions.q: In a potential divider with resistors $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$ across a supply $V$, the voltage across $R_{2}$ is:
questions.solution:
The voltage divides in proportion to resistance:

$V_{2} = \mathbf{\dfrac{R_{2}}{R_{1} + R_{2}}V}$.

Replacing one resistor with a thermistor or an LDR turns this into a sensing circuit whose output voltage varies with temperature or light.

questions.q: Find the charge (in C) passing when a current of $3$ A flows for $2$ minutes.
A wire of length $2$ m and cross-sectional area $0.5$ mm$^{2}$ has resistivity $1.7 \times 10^{-8}\,\Omega$ m. Find its resistance, in m$\Omega$.
questions.solution:
$R = \dfrac{\rho L}{A} = \dfrac{1.7 \times 10^{-8} \times 2}{0.5 \times 10^{-6}} = 6.8 \times 10^{-2}\,\Omega = \mathbf{68}$ m$\Omega$.

The area must be converted from mm$^{2}$ to m$^{2}$ — a factor of $10^{-6}$, and the usual place this goes wrong.

questions.q: A cell of emf $1.5$ V and internal resistance $0.5\,\Omega$ drives a current of $0.6$ A. Find the terminal potential difference, in V.
Find the power (in W) dissipated in a $20\,\Omega$ resistor carrying $0.5$ A.
A $12$ V supply is across resistors of $3\,\Omega$ and $9\,\Omega$ in series. Find the voltage (in V) across the $9\,\Omega$ resistor.
questions.solution:
$V = \dfrac{9}{12} \times 12 = \mathbf{9}$ V.

The larger resistance takes the larger share, in direct proportion.

questions.q: Derive $I = nAvq$ and use it to explain why a lamp lights instantly even though the drift velocity is only about $10^{-4}$ m/s.
questions.solution:
**Derivation.** Let $n$ be the number of free charge carriers per unit volume, $A$ the cross-sectional area, $v$ the drift velocity and $q$ the charge on each carrier.

In time $t$, every carrier moves a distance $vt$, so all the carriers within a cylinder of length $vt$ pass a chosen cross-section.

**Volume of that cylinder:** $Avt$

**Number of carriers in it:** $nAvt$

**Charge passing:** $Q = nAvtq$

$I = \dfrac{Q}{t} = \mathbf{nAvq}$

**Why the lamp lights at once.** The wire is **already full of free electrons**, everywhere along its length, before the switch is closed.

Closing the switch sets up an **electric field** along the wire, and that field propagates at close to the speed of light. Every electron in the circuit — including those already inside the lamp filament — begins to drift almost simultaneously.

No electron has to travel from the battery to the lamp for the lamp to light.

**The analogy:** a hosepipe already full of water. Turn on the tap and water comes out of the far end immediately, though any particular molecule takes a long time to make the journey.

**A consequence of the formula:** at a constriction in a wire, $A$ falls, so $v$ must rise to keep $I$ constant — which is why a thin fuse wire heats up far more than the cable it protects.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by internal resistance, describe an experiment to measure it and the emf of a cell, and say how the results are analysed.
questions.solution:
**Internal resistance** is the resistance of the cell's own materials — its electrolyte and electrodes. The current has to be driven through these as well as through the external circuit.

$\varepsilon = I(R + r)$, so the terminal voltage is $V = \varepsilon - Ir$.

The $Ir$ term is the 'lost volts', and it grows with the current drawn.

**The experiment.**

1. Connect the cell to a **variable resistor**, with an ammeter in series and a voltmeter across the cell's terminals.

2. Vary the resistance and record several pairs of $V$ and $I$.

3. Work quickly and open the switch between readings, so the cell does not warm up or run down — $r$ increases as a cell discharges.

**The analysis.** Compare $V = \varepsilon - Ir$ with $y = mx + c$:

Plot **$V$ (vertical) against $I$ (horizontal)**, giving a straight line.

• **Intercept on the $V$-axis** $= \varepsilon$, the emf — the terminal voltage when no current flows.

• **Gradient** $= -r$, so the internal resistance is the magnitude of the gradient.

**Why a graph rather than one reading.** A single pair of values would give $\varepsilon$ and $r$ only if a second pair were also taken, and the line averages out random errors while revealing any non-linearity.

**Why $r$ matters practically.** Maximum **power** is delivered to the load when $R = r$, and the cell's efficiency is then only $50\%$ — which is why a car battery is built with a very low internal resistance to deliver hundreds of amps to the starter motor.

questions.q: Explain how a potential divider works, and describe how to use one with a thermistor to switch on a heater when the temperature falls.
questions.solution:
**The principle.** Two resistors in series across a supply share the voltage in proportion to their resistances:

$V_{2} = \dfrac{R_{2}}{R_{1} + R_{2}}V$

The same current flows through both, so $V = IR$ makes the voltages proportional to the resistances.

**A temperature-sensing circuit.** Replace $R_{1}$ with a **thermistor** (an NTC type, whose resistance **falls** as temperature rises), and take the output across the fixed resistor $R_{2}$.

**When the temperature falls:**

1. The thermistor's resistance **rises**.

2. It therefore takes a larger share of the supply voltage.

3. The voltage across $R_{2}$ — the output — **falls**.

**To switch a heater on when it is cold**, that falling output is fed to a comparator or transistor arranged to trigger below a set threshold, which energises a **relay** carrying the heater's much larger current.

**Alternatively**, swapping the two components makes the output **rise** as it gets colder, which suits a circuit that triggers on a rising voltage. Which way round they go is decided by the switching electronics.

**Choosing $R_{2}$.** Make it comparable to the thermistor's resistance at the switching temperature, so the output changes most rapidly there.

**The same circuit with an LDR** in place of the thermistor switches a light on at dusk — one arrangement, two applications.

questions.q: State Kirchhoff's two laws, say what each expresses physically, and apply them to a circuit with two cells of emf $6$ V and $4$ V (internal resistances negligible) connected in parallel across a $2\,\Omega$ resistor.
questions.solution:
**First law (junction).** The sum of the currents entering a junction equals the sum leaving.

*Physically:* **conservation of charge** — charge cannot accumulate at a point.

**Second law (loop).** Around any closed loop, the sum of the emfs equals the sum of the $IR$ products.

*Physically:* **conservation of energy** — go round a loop and return to the same potential.

**The circuit.** Both cells are connected across the same $2\,\Omega$ resistor, so the potential difference across it is the same as across each cell.

With no internal resistance, the two cells would be forcing **different** potentials — $6$ V and $4$ V — across the same pair of points, which is impossible.

**That contradiction is itself the answer:** ideal cells of different emf cannot be connected in parallel. In practice the internal resistances are what make the situation physically consistent.

**With internal resistances $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$**, letting $V$ be the common terminal voltage:

$\dfrac{6 - V}{r_{1}} + \dfrac{4 - V}{r_{2}} = \dfrac{V}{2}$

For $r_{1} = r_{2} = 1\,\Omega$ this gives $V = 4$ V, a current of $2$ A through the resistor, $2$ A from the $6$ V cell and **zero** from the $4$ V cell.

**Push $r$ lower still** and the $4$ V cell begins to be **charged** by the $6$ V one — which is precisely why mismatched cells should never be paralleled, and why it is dangerous with rechargeable ones.

questions.q: Explain why the resistance of a metal increases with temperature while that of a thermistor decreases, and describe the $I$-$V$ characteristic of a filament lamp.
questions.solution:
**In a metal.** The number of free electrons is essentially fixed. Heating makes the lattice ions vibrate more violently, so electrons collide with them more often and the mean time between collisions falls.

$\rho = \dfrac{m}{ne^{2}\tau}$ — a smaller $\tau$ means a larger $\rho$, so **resistance rises**, roughly linearly over ordinary ranges.

**In a thermistor (NTC).** It is a semiconductor, and heating **liberates far more charge carriers** — the number density $n$ rises **exponentially**.

That swamps the increased scattering, so **resistance falls**, and steeply: a thermistor's resistance may change by a factor of ten over $50$°C, which is what makes it a sensitive temperature sensor.

**The filament lamp's $I$-$V$ characteristic.**

At low voltages the filament is cool and the graph is nearly **straight** — it behaves ohmically.

As the voltage rises the filament heats up, sometimes to $2500$°C, and its resistance climbs. The current therefore rises **less than proportionally**, so the graph **curves towards the voltage axis**.

The gradient $\dfrac{I}{V}$ decreases, meaning the resistance increases — by a factor of about ten between cold and operating temperature.

**A practical consequence:** the surge of current at switch-on, when the filament is still cold and its resistance low, is what usually destroys the bulb. Filament lamps nearly always fail at the moment they are switched on.
